messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 22-year-old African American man who came to treatment while working as a school principal, a role whose constant demands for calm leadership have become increasingly hard for him to carry. He lives with his girlfriend, who has urged him for months to talk to someone after seeing how shaken he becomes at night and how tense he is during the school day. When he speaks about what happened in childhood, he does not tell it as a smooth story. He reaches for it and loses it. He says that when he tries on purpose to remember the abuse by his caregiver, “it goes blank” or comes back only in broken pieces: a hallway, the sound of footsteps changing pace, a hand grabbing his shirt, the sudden certainty that something bad was about to happen. The fragments do not line up neatly for him. Yet when they come on their own, they do not feel distant or historical. They feel sharper than ordinary memory, as if the scene is happening in front of him rather than belonging to the past.

What he can describe is the atmosphere in which he grew up: a home ruled by unpredictability. He learned early that danger was often preceded by not knowing. A caregiver’s mood could shift without warning; a normal moment could become violent in seconds. For Kwame, that uncertainty became as frightening as the assaults themselves. Looking back, what stands out is not one single coherent episode but a series of vivid sensory shards linked by the same helpless expectation. He remembers trying to read the room, trying to tell from a voice or a look whether he was safe, and discovering again and again that he could not stop what was coming.

Those same qualities shape his life now. At school, where much of his day is spent moving between classrooms, staff conversations, and student crises, unpredictable situations are especially hard for him. If a teacher appears unexpectedly at his office door with an urgent problem, or a disagreement in the hallway escalates suddenly, he feels his whole body tighten before he has time to think. In those moments he is not describing a thought-out memory of childhood; instead there is an immediate sense of danger and an urgent need to get control of himself. Because he has come to believe that he might not be able to control his anger and could do something terrible, he works hard to keep himself contained. He steps out of meetings, keeps his office door closed when he can, and avoids situations that feel chaotic or volatile. Colleagues have begun to notice that he is more rigid than he used to be, more insistent on structure and advance notice, and less willing to tolerate surprises.

Old photos can unsettle him in a different way. Family pictures, school archive images from childhood events, even scrolling past certain photos on a phone can stop him cold. The image itself may not show abuse, but something about seeing his younger self or seeing adults posed as if everything were normal brings those disconnected pieces rushing close. He has learned to look away quickly or hand albums to someone else. At home, his girlfriend has noticed that he avoids conversations that might involve childhood memories, especially if there are pictures around. He says he hates the feeling of being pulled toward something he cannot fully remember and yet somehow relives too vividly.

Nights are often the worst. When he wakes from a nightmare, the residue lingers into the morning with unusual force. He may sit upright, drenched in fear, unsure at first where he is, with the emotional certainty that something bad is about to happen. On those mornings he arrives at school already braced, more watchful, more easily overwhelmed by the ordinary unpredictability of children and staff. He finds himself thinking that whatever was done to him changed him permanently for the worse. He worries that underneath his careful professionalism there is damage that cannot be repaired. Just as painful is his conviction that bad things still happen beyond his control; the old helplessness does not feel like a childhood feeling but like a fact about how the world works.

Over time these habits have narrowed his life. He keeps tight routines, prefers plans not to change, and pulls back when his girlfriend wants spontaneity or asks direct questions about his past. He is ashamed of how frightened he feels by things other people consider manageable, and even more ashamed of how much effort it takes to appear composed. He finally sought help after waking from a nightmare and going to work the next day only to find himself overwhelmed by a sudden conflict between students. He did not lose control, but the fear that he might lodged in him for the rest of the day. Sitting in therapy now, Kwame is most afraid that the part of him shaped by childhood violence is fixed and dangerous. At the same time, he is hoping that if he can understand why these moments feel so immediate and overpowering, he might stop living as if the next unpredictable turn will always end in harm.
